newsitem.title: USA: White House closing in on air standards decision.
newsitem.headline: White House closing in on air standards decision.

text.p: The White House is closing in on a decision on a controversial proposal to tighten air quality standards for soot and smog, sources from industry, environmental groups and Congress said Monday.

The next several days could be crucial in determining whether the White House will face the wrath of industries and support the Environmental Protection Agency's proposal to set stricter air standards, the sources said. The administration's other options are to delay new standards or seek a compromise.

"People are looking for puffs of white smoke from the Vice President's mansion," a Democratic House aide said, referring to the traditional sign of a decision in a papal election. Vice President Al Gore is regarded as a staunch supporter of EPA Administrator Carol Browner.

Gore so far has been quiet on the EPA proposal, which has pitted industries against health advocates and environmentalists. His spokesman said Gore did not plan to comment until the administration had decided on its position.
The EPA was expected to submit this week or early next week a final recommendation to the administration on adopting the agency's own proposal, which was offered in November.
The recommendation will take into account reviews by the White House National Economic Council, the White House Council on Environmental Quality, and other agencies and departments.

"The idea is that what EPA sends over will reflect much of the expertise from around the administration, but it's not necessarily an administration or consensus document," an administration official said, adding that it could be changed.
He said each part of the rule -- on ground-level ozone, or smog, and on tiny particulate matter, or soot -- had at least 10 "key variables" that must be considered.
The EPA proposed reducing the limit for smog to 0.08 parts per million, measured over eight hours, from the current 0.12 parts per million, measured for one hour.

It proposed setting a new standard to focus on tiny particles of less than 2.5 microns in diameter that come from industrial combustion and exhaust and may lodge deep in the lungs. Current regulations are geared to larger dust particles.
The EPA has estimated it would cost up to $8.5 billion annually to meet the new standards. Industry groups say the costs could be much higher.

Citizens for a Sound Economy, a pro-business group lobbying against tighter standards, estimated about 230 House members had signed letters opposing or expressing concerns about the proposal. Fewer senators are on record about it, but "Dear Colleague" letters are circulating.
Congress eventually could vote on the issue and would need two-thirds majorities to overrule the president.
